newsitem.title: CHINA: China stocks end up on strong sentiment.
newsitem.headline: China stocks end up on strong sentiment.

text.p: China stock indices ended sharply higher on Monday on strong sentiment boosted by the end of the annual reporting season, brokers said.
All Chinese listed firms have now released their 1996 annual reports, with results being generally within expectations, analysts said.
The Shanghai B index surged 5.598 points, or 6.14 percent, to 96.817 on turnover of $31.604 million.
Both overseas and domestic investors were seen snapping up blue chips and the three Pudong real estate shares due to confidence in the market outlook, brokers said.
"The market is on a bull run with most investors believing that the index is still comparatively low considering the A share performance," one broker said.
Market giant Shanghai Chlor Alkali was the star and traded the most actively on overseas institutional buying, rising $0.034, or 10.00 percent, limit-up to $0.374 on volume of 5.7 million shares.
Shenzhen's B ended sharply higher on active buying triggered by surges on Shanghai's B share market, brokers said.
The B index gained 4.87 points, or 2.76 percent, to end at 181.14 on turnover of HK$253.9 million.
"Shenzhen's advance was propelled by strong rises in Shanghai," an analyst with a major Chinese brokerage said.
"The macro-economic background looks better in 1997, from which listed firms are likely to benefit," the analyst said.
Analysts said Shenzhen's B share market was likely to maintain upward momentum to top the 200-point level this month.
Steep gains on Shenzhen and Shanghai's domestic A share markets despite Beijing's announcement of a market expansion plan also fuelled B share advances, brokers said.
Shenzhen's A share index climbed 18.66 points, or 3.81 percent, to close at 507.88 on turnover of 16.90 billion yuan.
Shanghai's A share index soared 56.800 points, or 3.90 percent, to 1,513.303 on turnover of 12.628 billion yuan.
The SSE30 blue chip index soared 200.515 points, or 5.03 percent, to 4,189.865 points.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the country's top securities watchdog, on Monday announced the addition of five billion yuan to the existing 10 billion yuan quota of new share issues for 1997 or later.
Analysts said the move was clearly aimed at reining in the bull run on China's stock markets by diverting funds out of existing shares into new issues.
Television tube maker Shenzhen SEG was the top gainer in Shenzhen's B share market, surging HK$0.78, or 8.67 percent, to HK$9.78 due to optimism over the company's 1997 earnings.
